client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. I can't seem to focus on any of my university assignments — I'll sit down to study and then just... zone out, or end up crying instead of getting anything done. I'm honestly not sure if talking about it is going to fix anything, but I figured I should at least try.
therapist: I'm really glad you reached out, and I want you to know that what you're going through — losing your grandmother and then trying to keep up with university life — is genuinely hard, and it makes complete sense that you're struggling to focus. Grief has a way of pulling us away from the present, and those moments of zoning out or crying are your mind and heart doing something very human. You don't have to be sure that talking will help — just being willing to try is enough for us to start from.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Thanks, that's... actually a little reassuring to hear. I think part of me expected you to just tell me to push through it or make a study schedule or something, so it helps that you're not dismissing how hard it's been. I guess I just feel guilty too, like I should be handling this better by now — it's been a whole month and I still can't get through a single lecture without my mind drifting back to her.
therapist: That guilt you're describing — the sense that you *should* be "over it" by now — is one of the most common and painful parts of grief, but it's not based in reality; there's no deadline on missing someone you loved. I'm also noticing that even as you say it's reassuring, there's something in how you're speaking that sounds quite tender and subdued, like part of you is still carrying a lot of weight. I'm curious — when you say you should be handling this better, whose voice does that feel like? Is it something you'd say to a friend in the same situation?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That's... a really uncomfortable question, actually. I think the voice is kind of mine, but also maybe my mum's a little — she's very much a "keep moving forward" type of person, and I think I absorbed that growing up. And no, I wouldn't say any of this to a friend, I'd probably tell them to be gentle with themselves, but somehow that feels different when it's me.
therapist: It's really insightful that you can already see the gap there — you'd offer a friend gentleness without hesitation, yet somehow you're holding yourself to a completely different standard, one that sounds like it was handed to you rather than chosen. That "keep moving forward" message can be a loving intention from a parent, but it can also make it hard to give yourself permission to simply *feel* something without turning it into a failure. I wonder — what do you think it would actually look like for you to treat yourself the way you'd treat that friend, even just for today?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to just say "okay, I'll be kinder to myself" — but honestly, I don't really know what that looks like in practice when I have a deadline tomorrow and I'm still not over losing her. Like, being gentle with myself sounds nice in theory, but it also feels like it might just be an excuse to not get anything done, and then I'll fall further behind and feel even worse.
therapist: That tension you're naming is really real — self-compassion isn't the same as giving up, but when you're already anxious about falling behind, it can genuinely *feel* that way. I notice there's an energy in how you're talking about this, like your mind is moving quite fast, maybe trying to solve several things at once — the grief, the deadline, the guilt — all at the same time. What if being kind to yourself tomorrow didn't mean skipping the assignment, but just meant doing it without also punishing yourself for not doing it perfectly or fast enough?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think I understand what you mean, but I'm not sure I even know how to notice when I'm punishing myself in the moment — it kind of just happens automatically, like I'll write one sentence and immediately think "this is terrible, she would have wanted better for you." And that's the other thing, my grandmother was really proud of me being at university, so now every time I struggle with my work it feels like I'm letting her down somehow, which makes everything so much heavier.
therapist: What you just shared feels like a really important piece — that her pride in you, which was such a loving thing, has now become a kind of pressure that sits right alongside your grief. That thought, "she would have wanted better for you," is worth gently examining, because it's taking something she felt — joy and pride in *you* — and turning it into a standard you can fail, which I don't think is what she actually gave you. I'm curious, when you picture her watching you struggle through this month, do you really think she'd be disappointed — or might she be feeling something else entirely?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: When I actually picture her face... no, I don't think she'd be disappointed. I think she'd probably be fussing over me, telling me to eat something and sleep more, which makes me want to cry just thinking about it. It's strange because that image feels true, but it doesn't automatically make the other thought go away — like I can hold both at the same time and the harsher one still has more weight somehow.
therapist: The image you just described — her fussing over you, wanting you fed and rested — that *is* her love for you, and the fact that it brought tears tells me some part of you recognises its truth deeply. What you're noticing, that the gentler image feels true but the harsher thought still carries more weight, is actually really common with grief; the critical voice has often had years of practice and doesn't step aside just because we've found a kinder one. But you've just done something important — you accessed her real voice, even briefly, and that's something we can keep coming back to.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hadn't thought about it that way — that I actually reached her real voice, even for a second. It does feel different from the critical thought, warmer somehow, even though it also hurts more. I guess I'm just worried that if I keep trying to access that image, it'll start to feel like I'm making things up or projecting what I want to hear rather than what she'd actually say.
therapist: That worry makes a lot of sense, but I'd gently push back on it — you didn't invent a flattering fantasy just now, you pictured something very specific and ordinary, her telling you to eat and sleep, which sounds much more like a memory than a wish. There's something worth noticing too in how you're speaking about this — there's a kind of aliveness in your voice when you talk about her, even through the pain, like she's still very present for you. That presence isn't you making things up; it's actually what tells us the most about who she really was to you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That actually... lands differently than I expected it to. You're right that it was specific — it wasn't like I imagined her saying something grand or profound, it was just so her, that practical fussing. I think I've been so focused on not falling apart that I haven't really let myself just remember her properly, and now I'm wondering if that's part of why everything feels so stuck.
therapist: What you just said feels like a real breakthrough — that avoiding falling apart might actually be part of what's keeping you stuck, because it's also keeping *her* at a distance. There's something tender in how you're speaking right now, like you're arriving somewhere that matters, and I want to honour that. I wonder if, somewhere small and safe, you might allow yourself a little time just to remember her — not to process or fix anything, just to let her be present with you again.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I like the idea of that, but I'm also a little scared of what happens if I just sit with the memories without trying to hold myself together — like, I have a feeling it might open something I won't be able to close again before I have to go back to normal life. And I live with three other people in a student house, so there's not really anywhere private where I can just... let myself feel things without worrying about someone walking in.
therapist: The fear that you'll open something you can't close is really understandable, but I want to offer a gentle reframe — grief doesn't actually work like a floodgate you lose control of forever, and most people find that allowing themselves to feel it in small doses is less overwhelming than the anticipation of it. The practical reality of not having private space is also genuinely worth taking seriously, not dismissing. I'm wondering if we could think together about what a small, bounded moment of remembering might look like — even something like ten minutes with headphones in, or a short walk outside — somewhere that gives you just enough of a container to feel safe.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: A walk outside actually feels more manageable than I expected — there's something about being in motion that might make it easier, like I wouldn't just be sitting there drowning in it. I think I could try that, maybe tomorrow morning before the deadline stress kicks in. I'm still a little nervous about it, but I suppose ten minutes isn't so long that I couldn't pull myself back together afterwards if I needed to.
therapist: It sounds like something has genuinely shifted for you just now — you came in today not sure if talking would help at all, and you're leaving with a small, concrete plan that actually feels like *yours*. I love that you noticed movement might help, that's real self-knowledge, and ten minutes tomorrow morning before the deadline is exactly the kind of gentle, bounded thing that honours both your grief and your very real responsibilities. Be patient with yourself when you go on that walk — there's no right way to remember her, and she'll meet you there however it unfolds.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
